content.title: About
content.content: Naan is a traditional Indian flatbread baked in a tandoor at very high heat. The dough is usually made from wheat flour, water, yeast, salt and sometimes yogurt or ghee, giving the crust a crisp bite and the interior a soft, slightly aromatic texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Naan is often served hot, brushed with butter right after baking.
A tandoor is a clay oven that can reach temperatures of 400 °C, imparting a distinctive smoky flavor and cooking the bread from both sides simultaneously.
There are many variations: garlic naan, cheese naan, naan topped with sesame or poppy seeds.
In India naan is traditionally eaten with curry, dal or kebabs, using it as a “spoon” for sauces.
The word “naan” comes from the Persian “nan,” meaning “bread.”

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Naan provides a quick source of energy thanks to its high content of complex carbohydrates.

items.title: Contains protein
items.content: Wheat flour in naan supplies plant‑based protein important for tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The dough contains B1, B2 and niacin, which support metabolic processes.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Naan provides iron, magnesium and phosphorus, essential for bone health and blood formation.

items.title: Easily digestible
items.content: Its thin structure and small crumb size aid rapid digestion.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Naan contains gluten, so it should be avoided by people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Because it can raise blood sugar quickly, people with diabetes should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Salt content
items.content: Traditional recipes often include salt; the amount can be reduced if needed.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve naan hot, tear or cut into pieces and brush with butter. It can be used as a base for sandwiches, wrapped around meat, vegetables or sauces, and as a “spoon” for curries and gravies.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh naan in a paper bag at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage, wrap tightly in foil and refrigerate for up to 5 days or freeze in an airtight bag for up to 2 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken wings are small pieces of chicken meat, usually fried or baked, served with a hot sauce. The product is ready‑to‑eat as it is precooked (code 872).

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wings are a popular bar and fast‑food snack worldwide.
Hot sauce may be based on chili, habanero, or Tabasco peppers.
Traditionally wings are marinated in spices before cooking to enhance flavor.
The United States hosts an annual "World's Best Chicken Wings" competition.
Wings contain more protein per gram than most other chicken parts.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Chicken meat provides a complete source of protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamin B6 and B12 support nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Suitable for low‑carb diets when the sauce is sugar‑free.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: Wings provide iron, zinc, and phosphorus important for blood and bone health.

items.title: Capsaicin may boost metabolism
items.content: The spicy sauce’s capsaicin can increase metabolic rate and promote satiety.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Hot sauces often contain a lot of salt; people with hypertension should limit intake.

items.title: Spicy sauce can irritate the stomach
items.content: Those with gastritis or ulcers should be cautious.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Fried wings can be calorie‑rich due to oil and sauce.

items.title: Risk of bacterial growth if stored improperly
items.content: Keeping the product above 4 °C for more than 2 hours increases the risk of contamination.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Wings are eaten hot as a snack, served with extra sauce, coleslaw, or celery sticks. Their hand‑held nature makes them popular at parties and sporting events.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the ready‑to‑eat product in the refrigerator at +4 °C for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight container at -18 °C for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of ≥ 75 °C before consumption.

content.title: About
content.content: Turkey heart is a muscular offal with a dense, springy texture and a rich meaty flavor. It is larger than a chicken heart and very lean. Turkey hearts are braised, boiled, fried, cooked on skewers, and added to stews, soups, and ground meat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: A turkey heart is noticeably larger than a chicken heart.
It is a muscle, so it needs either long braising or thin slicing.
Turkey heart is one of the leanest offal cuts.
Before cooking, fat, vessels, and blood clots are trimmed off.
Turkey hearts are braised for about thirty to forty minutes to become tender.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Turkey heart provides high-quality protein with modest fat.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Iron is well absorbed and is needed for oxygen transport.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is important for the nervous system and the formation of blood cells.

items.title: Contains zinc and selenium
items.content: These nutrients support immunity and cell protection.

items.title: Contains coenzyme Q10
items.content: Coenzyme Q10 helps cells produce energy.

items.title: Cholesterol
items.content: Offal contains cholesterol, so people with high cholesterol should limit portions.

items.title: Gout
items.content: Hearts contain purines, which may trigger gout attacks.

items.title: Undercooked meat
items.content: Undercooked hearts may contain Salmonella and Campylobacter; they should be cooked until fully done.

items.title: Fat and salt when cooked
items.content: Grilling with a marinade or frying in breading adds a lot of fat and salt to the dish.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Rinse the hearts, trim off the fat, vessels, and blood clots, and slice. Braise them with sour cream and onion for about 30–40 minutes until tender, fry them, thread on skewers and grill, or add to stews and soups. Cook until fully done.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store raw hearts in the refrigerator in a covered container for one to two days or freeze them. Thaw in the refrigerator. Keep cooked hearts in the refrigerator for three to four days.

venison-or-deer-noodles-and-vegetables-i.title: Venison with Noodles and Vegetables in Tomato Sauce

content.title: About
content.content: The dish combines tender venison, noodles, carrots, broccoli and/or dark‑green leafy vegetables, all tossed in a flavorful tomato‑based sauce. Venison is a lean source of protein, while the vegetables add vitamins, minerals and fiber.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Venison contains less fat than beef and is rich in iron and zinc.
Tomatoes in the sauce provide lycopene, a powerful antioxidant.
Broccoli is one of the most nutrient‑dense vegetables, high in vitamin C and K.
Al dente noodles retain their shape and absorb the sauce quickly.
Dark‑green leafy greens such as spinach or kale are high in folate and B‑vitamins.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Venison supplies complete protein needed for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with many other meats, venison has lower saturated fat, supporting heart health.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: The vegetables contribute vitamins A, C, K, folate, potassium and magnesium for overall wellbeing.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Lycopene from tomatoes and phytochemicals from broccoli help combat free radicals.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Carrots, broccoli and leafy greens boost fiber content, aiding digestion.

items.title: Allergy to game meat
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to venison.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Venison is relatively high in purines, which can be an issue for people with gout.

items.title: Sodium in sauce
items.content: Tomato sauces often contain added salt; those with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Cooking sensitivity
items.content: Venison can become dry if overcooked, so careful timing is required.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, mixing the noodles with the sauce, then adding sliced venison and vegetables. Garnish with fresh herbs or grated Parmesan if desired. Ideal as a main course for lunch or dinner.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Store unused ingredients separately: raw venison in the freezer, noodles and vegetables in the fridge.
